--- title: "Three Kingdoms" author: "DK" date: "2026-10-21" categories: [dynasties] --- During my traveling years, I stopped off in Korea on my way home from China. My father’s youngest brother—작은아버지, who was 43 at the time—met me in Seoul and took me around the city. As we walked through the grand courtyards of Gyeongbokgung, the main palace, we shared a realization: despite all the painted timber and sprawling stone grounds, our lives were undeniably better than those of the Joseon kings. At the time, Korea’s per capita GDP stood around $12,841. In the years since, that number has nearly tripled to over $37,000. Even after accounting for inflation, the real growth of the nation has more than doubled. If we were richer than kings then, we live like deities now—enjoying health, warmth, mobility, and comfort that no ancient throne could ever grant. --- Here are three distinct narrative angles you can choose from for your blog post about visiting the three royal palaces of Seoul (Gyeongbokgung, Changdeokgung, and Deoksugung). --- ### Angle 1: The Personal Angle — *Three Palaces, Three Eras of Wealth* * **The Frame:** A reflective family narrative connecting the Joseon kings, your uncle’s generation during your initial visit, and the present day. * **How It Works:** You use each palace to anchor a different layer of prosperity: * **Gyeongbokgung (The Symbol of Power):** The initial walk with your 43-year-old uncle where you both realized that modern commoners live better than historical monarchs. * **Changdeokgung (The Secret Garden & Quality of Life):** Reflecting on comfort, nature, and health—things ancient kings struggled to secure despite their grand courtyards. * **Deoksugung (The Bridge to Modernity):** Bringing in the hard economic numbers (GDP growing from $12,841 to $37,412, a real growth of +178%) to show how dramatically ordinary life has surpassed royal luxury in just a single generation. ### Angle 2: The Philosophical Angle — *Living Like Kings (Without the Crown)* * **The Frame:** A meditation on the illusion of grand architecture vs. the reality of everyday human comfort. * **How It Works:** The grand wooden pillars and stone courtyards were designed to show absolute authority, yet Joseon kings lacked simple daily comforts: warm indoor plumbing, modern medicine, global food, and swift transport. * **The Takeaway:** True wealth isn't measured in court servants or sprawling throne halls; it's measured in the quiet, friction-free conveniences of modern daily life. ### Angle 3: The Economic Angle — *The 2.9× Revolution* * **The Frame:** A story of exponential progress, using the three palaces as a backdrop for Korea’s remarkable transformation. * **How It Works:** Contrast the static, ancient stone of the palaces with the dynamic growth of Seoul outside their walls. Looking back at your stopover from China, you examine how a country's real purchasing power more than doubled, turning what was once a quiet reflection into a concrete mathematical reality. --- ### Draft: The Full Blog Post *(Framed around Angle 1)* Years ago, during my traveling years, I made a stopover in Korea on my way home from China. My father’s youngest brother—my uncle, who was 43 at the time—met me in Seoul and offered to show me around the capital. Our first stop was Gyeongbokgung, the grand main palace of the Joseon Dynasty. As we walked past the sweeping curved roofs and through the sprawling stone courtyards, we began talking about what life must have been like behind those historic gates. Despite the grand scale and royal authority, we reached a shared, quiet realization: our lives as ordinary citizens were undeniably better than those of the Joseon kings. A king had servants, but he had no central heating, no hot running water, no modern medicine, and no way to travel across the world in a matter of hours. His world was magnificent, but tight and fragile. From Gyeongbokgung, we moved on to Changdeokgung, famous for its harmonious integration with nature and its famous Secret Garden. Standing under the ancient trees, it became even clearer that true quality of life isn't about power—it is about comfort, health, and peace of mind. The kings built gardens to escape the pressures of court life, yet their daily existence was constrained by politics, disease, and the limitations of their time. Finally, we visited Deoksugung, a palace uniquely situated alongside modern Western-style stone buildings, standing right in the bustling heart of downtown Seoul. It serves as a physical bridge between old Korea and the modern era. When my uncle and I shared that conversation at Gyeongbokgung, Korea’s per capita GDP stood around $12,841. In the years since, that figure has grown 2.9 times to $37,412. Even after adjusting for cumulative inflation, total real GDP growth has surged by 178%. If we were already living better than kings back when I first visited, today we live with a level of abundance, health, and freedom that no Joseon monarch could have purchased with all the gold in the royal treasury. The stone walls of Seoul's royal palaces once kept the world out, preserving luxury for a select few. Today, standing outside those same walls in a thriving, modern city, you realize the greatest achievement isn't the thrones preserved inside—it is the fact that everyday life outside the gates has made kings of us all. --- During my traveling years, I stopped off in Korea on the way home from China.
